Apply ice packs if swelling is present
Rest and avoid triggers that worsen discomfort
First Few Days: Swelling and pain should begin to improve if on antibiotics — improvement is usually noticeable within 24–48 hours
Complete all antibiotic courses even if feeling better
First Week: Attend your follow-up appointment to complete definitive treatment
Long-Term Care: Follow through with the definitive treatment plan (root canal, crown, extraction, etc.)
Regular dental care helps prevent future emergencies

procedures.name: Oral Cancer Screening
procedures.summary: A routine visual and physical examination that checks for early signs of oral cancer or precancerous changes in the mouth.
procedures.overview: An oral cancer screening is a quick, painless examination performed by your dentist to check for signs of cancer or precancerous conditions in the mouth, throat, and lips. It's typically performed as part of a routine dental examination and is one of the most valuable early-detection tools available.
procedures.whyNeeded: Oral cancer is significantly more treatable when detected early. Risk factors include tobacco use, heavy alcohol consumption, HPV infection, prolonged sun exposure (lip cancer), and a personal history of oral cancer. Annual screenings allow suspicious changes to be identified and evaluated before they progress.

steps.title: Visual examination
steps.text: The dentist examines all soft tissue surfaces inside your mouth — lips, cheeks, gums, tongue, floor of mouth, and roof of mouth — looking for unusual color changes, lumps, or sores.

steps.title: Manual palpation
steps.text: The dentist gently presses on tissues to feel for lumps, hardness, or tenderness that may not be visible.

steps.title: Neck exam
steps.text: The lymph nodes in the neck are gently palpated for unusual enlargement.

steps.title: Adjunctive tools (optional)
steps.text: Special lights or dyes may be used to highlight tissue irregularities not visible to the naked eye.

steps.title: Documentation and referral
steps.text: Any suspicious findings are documented. A biopsy referral may be arranged if needed — early evaluation is always the safest approach.

procedures.comfort: Oral cancer screening is entirely painless and non-invasive. It adds just a few minutes to your regular dental appointment.
benefits: Early detection dramatically improves survival rates
Completely painless and non-invasive
Takes only minutes as part of your routine exam
Provides peace of mind
Identifies early precancerous changes when intervention is most effective
procedures.risks: No risks from the screening itself. Suspicious lesions will require a biopsy to confirm whether they are concerning — this is a follow-up procedure with minimal risk.

First 24 Hours: No aftercare required
First Few Days: Report any new sores, lumps, or changes to your dentist promptly
First Week: Normal routine
Long-Term Care: Include oral cancer screening at every dental examination
Perform monthly self-examinations of your mouth at home — look and feel for changes
Reduce risk factors: avoid tobacco, limit alcohol, ask your doctor about HPV vaccination

procedures.name: Inlay / Onlay
procedures.summary: Custom-made ceramic or gold restorations that fit precisely within or over damaged tooth cusps — stronger than a filling, less invasive than a crown.
procedures.overview: Inlays and onlays are custom-made restorations fabricated in a dental laboratory from porcelain, ceramic, composite resin, or gold. An inlay fits within the cusps of a tooth like a puzzle piece, while an onlay extends to cover one or more cusps. They're ideal for teeth with moderate damage — too extensive for a filling but not requiring a full crown.
procedures.whyNeeded: When tooth damage or decay is too large for a filling to reliably repair, but the remaining tooth structure is strong enough that a full crown isn't necessary, an inlay or onlay provides the perfect middle ground. They restore function and aesthetics with outstanding long-term durability.

steps.title: Preparation
steps.text: The decayed or damaged tissue is removed and the tooth is prepared under local anesthesia.

steps.title: Impression
steps.text: A detailed mold is sent to the laboratory for fabrication.

steps.title: Temporary restoration
steps.text: A temporary filling protects the tooth between visits.

steps.title: Fitting and bonding
steps.text: The completed restoration is fitted, adjusted for bit, and permanently bonded.

procedures.comfort: Performed under local anesthesia. Post-treatment sensitivity is mild and resolves within a week.
benefits: More durable than traditional fillings
Preserves more natural tooth structure than a crown
Excellent fit and seal — less likely to harbor bacteria
Long-lasting — can last 20+ years with proper care
Available in tooth-colored materials for a natural appearance
procedures.risks: Rare possibility of post-placement sensitivity or the need for minor bite adjustments.

First 24 Hours: Avoid very hard or sticky foods on the new restoration
First Few Days: Mild sensitivity is normal and will resolve
First Week: The restoration should feel natural
Long-Term Care: Brush and floss normally — these restorations are very strong
Include in regular dental examinations

procedures.name: Apicoectomy
procedures.summary: A minor surgical procedure that removes the tip of a tooth's root and surrounding infected tissue when a conventional root canal cannot resolve the infection.
procedures.overview: An apicoectomy is a minor oral surgery performed when a previous root canal hasn't fully resolved an infection at the root tip (apex) of a tooth. The procedure removes the last few millimeters of the root end along with any infected tissue, and seals the root end with a small filling.
procedures.whyNeeded: Sometimes root canals fail due to complex root anatomy, reinfection, cysts, or persistent inflammation at the root tip. When retreatment isn't possible or hasn't worked, an apicoectomy gives the tooth a second chance to heal without extraction.

steps.title: Anesthesia
steps.text: Local anesthesia thoroughly numbs the area. Sedation is available.

steps.title: Incision and flap
steps.text: A small incision in the gum exposes the bone near the root tip.

steps.title: Bone access
steps.text: A small window in the bone is created to reach the root tip.

steps.title: Root end removal
steps.text: The infected root tip (approximately 3mm) and surrounding tissue are removed.

steps.title: Root end filling
steps.text: A small filling seals the root end to prevent future bacterial entry.

steps.title: Closure
steps.text: The gum flap is sutured back into place.

procedures.comfort: The procedure is comfortable under local anesthesia. Post-surgical soreness, swelling, and mild bruising are normal for several days.
benefits: Saves a tooth that would otherwise require extraction
Resolves persistent infection when conventional retreatment isn't sufficient
High success rate — approximately 85–90%
Preserves the natural tooth and avoids the need for an implant or bridge
procedures.risks: Considerations include possible temporary numbness near the treated root, slow healing in smokers or patients with compromised immunity, and rare treatment failure requiring eventual extraction.

First 24 Hours: Rest; apply ice packs for swelling
Soft diet only
Take prescribed medications
First Few Days: Salt water rinses after 24 hours
Avoid strenuous activity for 3–5 days
Bruising and swelling are expected and will resolve
First Week: Suture removal at follow-up appointment
Soreness should steadily decrease
Long-Term Care: Follow-up X-rays at 6 months and 1 year to confirm healing
The treated tooth should function normally

procedures.name: Frenectomy
procedures.summary: A minor surgical procedure that removes or modifies a frenum — a small fold of tissue that may restrict tongue or lip movement, or cause a gap between teeth.
procedures.overview: A frenectomy removes or modifies a frenum — a small band of tissue connecting the tongue to the floor of the mouth (lingual frenum) or the upper lip to the gum (labial frenum). When a frenum is unusually tight or positioned, it can cause tongue-tie, restricted lip movement, gaps between front teeth, or nursing difficulties in infants.
procedures.whyNeeded: A labial frenectomy is often recommended when a thick frenum creates or maintains a gap between upper front teeth (diastema). A lingual frenectomy (tongue-tie release) is performed when restricted tongue movement affects speech, swallowing, breastfeeding, or oral hygiene.

steps.title: Local anesthesia or topical gel
steps.text: The area is numbed. Infants may require only topical anesthetic.

steps.title: Tissue removal
steps.text: The frenum is removed or modified using a scalpel, scissors, or laser.

steps.title: Closure
steps.text: Small sutures close the wound. Laser procedures may require no sutures.

procedures.comfort: The procedure is quick and performed under local anesthesia. Post-procedure discomfort is typically mild and short-lived — most patients describe it as similar to a canker sore.
benefits: Resolves tongue-tie and associated speech/swallowing issues
Closes the gap between upper front teeth (often in combination with orthodontics)
Improves oral hygiene access
Improves breastfeeding in infants
Quick recovery
procedures.risks: Very low-risk. Minor bleeding, temporary soreness, and rare re-attachment (requiring revision) are possible.

First 24 Hours: Cool soft diet
Take OTC pain reliever as needed
Gently rinse with salt water
First Few Days: Perform stretching exercises if instructed — this prevents re-attachment
Avoid tobacco and mouthwash containing alcohol
First Week: Healing is rapid; most patients feel normal within a week
Long-Term Care: For tongue-tie release in children: myofunctional therapy or speech therapy may be recommended to maximize the functional benefit

procedures.name: TMJ Splint / Guard
procedures.summary: A custom oral appliance that repositions the jaw to reduce pain, clicking, and strain associated with temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders.
procedures.overview: A TMJ splint (also called an occlusal splint or stabilization appliance) is a custom-fitted oral device worn over the teeth to reduce stress on the temporomandibular joint, relax jaw muscles, and alleviate symptoms of TMJ disorder (TMD). It's typically worn at night but may also be recommended for daytime use in severe cases.
procedures.whyNeeded: TMJ disorders cause pain in the jaw joint and surrounding muscles, clicking or popping sounds, limited jaw opening, headaches, and neck pain. Untreated, chronic clenching and grinding can cause progressive joint damage, tooth wear, and worsening symptoms. A splint addresses the mechanical source of the problem.

steps.title: TMJ evaluation
steps.text: A thorough assessment of jaw movement, muscle tenderness, joint sounds, and bite relationship.

steps.title: Impressions
steps.text: Detailed impressions are sent to a lab where the splint is fabricated to precise specifications.

steps.title: Delivery and calibration
steps.text: The splint is adjusted so your bite is balanced and comfortable in the appliance.

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.text: Regular adjustments and monitoring ensure the splint continues to provide therapeutic benefit.

procedures.comfort: TMJ splints take 1–2 weeks to adapt to. Most patients begin noticing symptom improvement within 2–4 weeks of consistent use.
benefits: Reduces jaw muscle pain and fatigue
Decreases headaches and neck tension
Protects teeth from grinding damage
May improve joint clicking or locking over time
Non-invasive — no surgery required
procedures.risks: A poorly fitted splint can worsen symptoms. Custom-fabricated appliances from a trained dentist are essential. Some patients require additional treatments (physical therapy, stress management) for full resolution.

First 24 Hours: Wear the splint as directed, typically at night
First Few Days: Initial awareness of the appliance is normal
Some patients notice mild jaw muscle soreness initially — this improves
First Week: Continue wearing consistently for best results
Long-Term Care: Clean the splint daily with a soft toothbrush and cool water
Attend follow-up appointments — splints require periodic calibration as symptoms improve
Pair with jaw exercises, stress reduction, and heat therapy for comprehensive management

procedures.name: Sinus Lift
procedures.summary: A bone grafting procedure that adds bone to the upper jaw below the sinus floor, creating the vertical bone height needed for upper implants.
procedures.overview: A sinus lift (sinus augmentation) is a bone grafting procedure performed when the upper jaw lacks sufficient bone height beneath the maxillary sinuses to support dental implants. Bone graft material is placed between the jawbone and the sinus membrane, which is gently lifted to create space. Over several months, this grafted material integrates into your own bone.
procedures.whyNeeded: When upper back teeth are lost, the sinus cavity can expand downward and bone naturally resorbs, leaving insufficient bone for implant placement. A sinus lift creates the necessary bone volume, making implants possible where they otherwise couldn't be placed.

steps.title: Anesthesia
steps.text: Local anesthesia with sedation options. IV sedation is common for this procedure.

steps.title: Incision
steps.text: A small incision in the upper gum area exposes the lateral wall of the sinus.

steps.title: Window creation
steps.text: A small opening is created in the bone to access the sinus membrane.

steps.title: Membrane elevation
steps.text: The sinus membrane is gently lifted upward, creating a space beneath it.

steps.title: Graft placement
steps.text: Bone graft material fills the created space.

steps.title: Closure and healing
steps.text: The incision is closed. Bone integration takes 4–9 months before implants can be placed.

procedures.comfort: Performed under local anesthesia with sedation available. Post-surgical swelling and discomfort are managed with prescribed medications. Some patients experience temporary sinus congestion.
benefits: Enables implant placement in upper jaw where bone is deficient
High success rate when performed by experienced practitioners
Long-lasting results once integration is complete
procedures.risks: Risks include sinus membrane perforation (can usually be repaired during the procedure), infection, and incomplete graft integration. Smokers face significantly higher complication rates.

First 24 Hours: Avoid blowing your nose — pressure can dislodge the graft
Sneeze with mouth open
Sleep with head slightly elevated
Apply ice packs for swelling
First Few Days: Take all prescribed medications
Use nasal decongestant spray as directed to prevent sinus congestion
Eat soft foods; avoid the surgical side
First Week: Do not blow your nose vigorously for 2 weeks
Avoid strenuous activity for 1 week
Long-Term Care: Follow-up imaging at 4–6 months to evaluate graft integration before implant placement
Do not smoke — it significantly compromises healing

procedures.name: Root Canal Retreatment
procedures.summary: A second root canal procedure that opens and re-treats a previously treated tooth where infection or pain has returned.
procedures.overview: Root canal retreatment involves reopening a previously root-canal-treated tooth, removing the old filling material, cleaning the canals thoroughly, and re-sealing them. It's performed when a previous root canal has not fully healed, when new infection develops, or when previously inaccessible canals are identified.
procedures.whyNeeded: Root canals can occasionally fail due to: complex canal anatomy that wasn't fully cleaned the first time; contamination of the filling material over time; a new cavity allowing bacteria to re-enter the sealed tooth; or a delayed crown placement. Retreatment gives the tooth a second chance at healing.

steps.title: Anesthesia
steps.text: Local anesthesia provides complete comfort throughout.

steps.title: Crown or filling removal
steps.text: The existing crown or filling over the tooth is removed to access the root canals.

steps.title: Removal of old filling material
steps.text: The gutta-percha (rubber-like filling) from the previous root canal is carefully removed using small instruments.

steps.title: Thorough cleaning
steps.text: All canals are re-examined, any missed canals are located, and the entire canal system is cleaned and shaped with antimicrobial irrigation.

steps.title: Re-sealing
steps.text: Fresh gutta-percha seals the canals and the tooth is sealed temporarily or with a new restoration.

procedures.comfort: Retreatment is performed under local anesthesia and is typically comparable in comfort to the original procedure. Post-treatment soreness is expected for a few days.
benefits: Saves the natural tooth and avoids extraction
Addresses persistent infection or pain
High success rate — comparable to initial root canal treatment
Preserves the existing crown in many cases
procedures.risks: Occasionally, complex post and core restorations make canal access difficult. Very rarely, canal calcification prevents complete retreatment. In these cases, apicoectomy or extraction may be alternative options.

First 24 Hours: Avoid chewing on the treated tooth
Take recommended pain relievers
First Few Days: Soreness when biting is expected and should improve daily
First Week: Contact your dentist if pain worsens after day 3
Long-Term Care: Have a new crown placed as recommended to protect the retreated tooth
